utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We couldn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be noted. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just, Your Honours, I'm sorry. Good morning -- good afternoon. I see on the transcript there was no interpretation of the witness. I didn't get it on my headphones either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, do you hear me? Do you follow the proceedings in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Nicholls. Ah-ha, the witness's declaration hasn't been reflected in the transcript. Sorry for your inconvenience, but could you repeat your declaration, please. Probably your microphone was not on at the time and it was not interpreted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to move closer to the mike. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, I'm just going to ask you a few questions and please remember not to say your name as we talk today. Okay?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First of all, could I please have 65 ter 90263 which is the witness's statement on the screen, and it should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, now just a very few questions concerning this statement. Do you remember that you and I met for the first time just this last Monday?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you remember that we went through a statement together that day and that you signed the statement at the end?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Looking at the statement in front of you on the screen, without saying your name out loud, under where it says "witness information," could you just please confirm to the Trial Chamber that your name is written there.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I have to ask you two more questions about the statement. You recall it was read back to you on Monday, before you signed it, off the computer screen. Can you confirm to the Trial Chamber that this statement is accurate?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you also please confirm that if you were asked questions about the same topics that are in the statement today, that your answers on those topics, the information you gave, would be the same as what we have in the statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ask to admit the statement under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before I assign the exhibit number to this, I make a correction to the exhibit list from yesterday. 65 ter number 00749 was assigned Exhibit P3205; in fact, it should be Exhibit P3202. And as far as this particular exhibit is concerned, 65 ter 90263, that will be Exhibit P3205, under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. And before I continue, I should note there is one typographical error on the cover of the statement where it says language used in interview at the bottom, it says "English." That should be "English and B/C/S" because both languages were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, before we move on further. Sir, I take it that you were explained as to the effect of the protective measures you were given. Do you understand you will be called rather by your pseudonym, and your voice and image will not be broadcast, and when we are going to deal with the information that may reveal your identity, we will go into private session, which means the people outside this courtroom cannot follow the proceedings at all. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will now read a brief summary of the statement for the public. The witness is a Muslim man who lived in Bratunac with his family before the war. Tensions rose between Muslims and Serbs in Bratunac municipality prior to the outbreak of the war in 1992. Paramilitary troops, Arkan's men, and Seselj's men arrived in Bratunac on the 17th of April, 1992. JNA soldiers also arrived and Muslim homes were broken into and looted. In late April 1992, Muslims in Bratunac were required to sign oaths of loyalty to the Serb authorities in Bratunac and the witness personally signed such an oath. On 10 May, the witness and his family, along with thousands of others -- of people, Muslim people from Bratunac, were detained in the stadium in Bratunac town. The witness was separated from his family, from his wife and from his children. Women and children held at the stadium were taken to Tuzla on buses. The witness and hundreds of other men were detained at the Vuk Karadzic school and hangar in Bratunac. The witness was held at the school for three days. During this time, he saw guards beating and murdering prisoners. Men were beaten to death, stabbed, and shot. And the witness was beaten when he was held at the Vuk Karadzic school. After three days, most of the men held at the school were taken by truck to Pale. There they were held in a sports hall for three days. In Pale, in the sports hall, the conditions were better and the witness did not observe any murders, but some prisoners were beaten. Ultimately, the prisoners and the witness were taken from Pale in trucks to Visoko and released. That's the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I have just a few questions for you, and the first thing I want to do is show you a video which is 65 ter 40115A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll play it in Sanction, but I will ask to go into private session, Your Honours, for the witness's comments on the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, would you like to view the video in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've struggled to find a way to deal with it. I think the best is to view it in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. May the Chamber go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Nicholls, you are tendering that video?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be admitted in public?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be done, Exhibit P3206. And you're tendering the associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I can read those numbers, if you like. That would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Six of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the sixth one is a video that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, six including the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. They will be all admitted and given numbers in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should say, if I may, that 618 should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 609 should be under seal, and 608 should be under seal, and I can explain why in private session, if necessary. 23447, I think should also be under seal, and that was a new document not on our 65 ter list which came up when I met the witness on Monday. I've spoken to Mr. Robinson about it. He does not objected to it being entered -- to it being tendered. I thank him for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So the addition of the document was granted and will be admitted. Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Sir, you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. Good afternoon, Excellencies. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am addressing you as Mr. Witness because of the protective measures, and I hope I will not make an error and address you by your real name. But please bear in mind that that wouldn't be intentional if that happened because that would be a mere mistake. (redacted) (redacted) is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who drafted the answers that you gave?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: For the most part, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, you are referring -- you are going to refer to lines 17 and 18?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, and if I could go into private session for just one minute. I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic, bearing that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you say a moment ago? What formulated your answers? Who chose the words?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, nobody chose the words. I gave answers on my own, the way I saw things, and I actually saw very little. There were a great deal of things going on, but I just said what it was that I saw. And in some cases, I spoke about the things I heard, too. At any rate, nobody formulated my answers or suggested what I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This cross-examination will be conducted in that sense. We will try to spell out precisely what we can take as facts, things you have seen yourself, and what are the things that you heard of. But I would be interested in hearing who it was that lived in Bratunac, which ethnic community, which people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: For the most part, Muslims and Serbs: 64 per cent Muslims; 32 per cent Serbs; a few others that characterised themselves as "others." At any rate, it was a very small, negligible number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did it happen then that you kept repeating Muslims and non-Serbs? Who are these non-Serbs of yours in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, those persons who characterised themselves as Yugoslavs, Roma, there were a few Croats as well, a negligible number. Basically, those were the people who were considered as "others."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But these Yugoslavs, it doesn't mean that they were non-Serbs. I wonder how you got this term "non-Serbs." Did you invent it or was it suggested by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: No one formulated it. I said it of my own free will. I meant people who were not Serbs and who were not Muslims either, in terms of their orientation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the population of your village?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: In my local commune -- my local commune was not a village, it was called a local commune. It was a wider area. I could never actually establish that. I never know the exact figure. If you would like to hear my free assessment, I can provide it, but it's probably not going to be very accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in your village itself?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: It was not a village. Your Honours, that was a town, a suburb. I cannot say in any way that this is a limited number of houses. Well, it depends on what we are going to take into account and what we are going to consider a village. (redacted) went from the outskirts of town, and most of the area it comprised, it was, say, 2.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha, and the majority population was Muslim there; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were Serbs there as well; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: There were Serbs but very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for pausing and I'm asking you to do the same thing because this has to do with interpretation. Are you familiar with your municipality, its structure, who lives where and things like that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, I know enough, quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're going to ask you to show us -- actually, I did turn on my microphone. Can the interpreter hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to show you a map, and we are going to identify these settlements so that it would be easier for the Trial Chamber to follow things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D225. Could we please have that in e-court. Thank you. Could we please zoom in on the middle part of the right-hand side, on the very right. Now, you will see in the middle of the picture Bratunac and Srebrenica. So could we please zoom in there. It's Bratunac-Srebrenica and that part of Serbia that is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to zoom in further, pursuant to Mr. Karadzic's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we put that in the centre, if possible, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, to the right -- to the other way -- further. We see Bratunac and Srebrenica on the right side part, why don't we put it in the centre -- no, no, the other way around, further, further, and we zoom in further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the very right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, move it further. I think that -- is that -- does that suit you, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will do. Thank you. I think this will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you see this dark line that denotes the border of the municipality of Bratunac and the thin lines show the borders of villages?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. I see these lines showing the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Bratunac seems to resemble a lizard, a salamander, if you wish, with a head on one side and a long tail on the other side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I have no idea how come you think it resembles that, but maybe you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark Skelani with the map -- with the pen that you've been provided with.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I was in Skelani personally. Skelani is right by the Drina, upstream from Bratunac, 45 or 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I ask the assistance with the pencil, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that is Skelani is somewhere here, right on the Drina River, on the border with Serbia. On this map -- actually, Skelani is on Drina and on the border with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But is it not these blue areas at the very horn, if you wish, on the extreme right where the municipality of Bratunac starts by the Drina?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Skelani belongs to the municipality of Srebrenica, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that horn that is blue. And do you know that it used to be a municipality, and during the war it was again the municipality of Skelani?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Consisting of these Serb villages from Bratunac and Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I heard something like that, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now mark Glogova with a G. You were in the army, you are familiar with maps.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, in the army, yes. Glogova is not far away from Bratunac, perhaps 10 kilometres away. First, it's the village of Hranica [phoen], then there's a Serb village, then Hranca, and then Glogova, 10, 12 kilometres -- Glogova was a big village and basically populated by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak into the microphone, we can no longer hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the green area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say anything further after saying Glogova was a big village and basically populated by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say anything else. I know Glogova very well. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. When you answer the question, could you kindly speak to the microphone so that the interpreters can follow you. Thank you. Let us continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, not to interrupt, but perhaps a redaction in line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Witness, to note this point that shows the town of Bratunac and then to the north-west. Is that the first Serb village and then Hranca and then Glogova surrounded by Serb villages? And can you place number 1 by Bratunac; 2 by the Serb village; 3 by Hranca; 4 by Glogova using that pen?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Number 1, that's the town of Bratunac; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next to the west is the Serb village?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it possible to move back the microphone, a bit further. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that Serb village with 2, Hranca; that is the next one, by 3; and Glogova, the largest light area by 4, if those are the villages concerned.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Glogova is? Do you see it there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I'm not sure I see it. What colour? What colour denotes which population?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dark blue, Serbs; light green, Muslims. And when you move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think we are -- we seem to be losing the point when the witness is not able to identify where a certain village is. We can do this by the exercise of comparing two maps later on --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you something, Mr. Witness: Is it correct that an agreement had been reached and signed on establishing two municipalities out of Bratunac; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: The only correct thing in Bratunac was that an agreement was reached to divide the police. As for two municipalities, I had never heard of an agreement like that. The Serbs had asked for that kind of thing, but I have no knowledge of any agreement being reached to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were in the leadership of that party, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Don't say where.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: No. I was sort of a chairman in an area, but I also worked the first shift. So I was always absent during the day. My engagement in that government was virtually nil.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But did you hear of the Serbs asking for the establishment of two municipalities, one Serb and one Muslim, and also establishing a Serb MUP and a Muslim MUP, respectively, and that Serb policemen go to Serb villages and Muslim policemen to Muslim villages, and would these villages be in the Muslim municipality and the Serb villages in the Serb municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I just heard once of the Serbs asking for this division. This was one particular variant. However, nothing was done about it. I don't know what kind of maps were discussed, which villages should go where, I did not participate in that, and I don't know about anybody saying anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We had a higher official of your party here, the man who had signed that agreement. Is it correct that the division of the MUP was not something that you decided upon; rather, it had been agreed at central level, the question of establishing municipalities and local communes is a municipal affair. Did you agree that as for the MUP, a decision had been made at central level, at the level of the ministry itself?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I had not heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we remove this map. We're not going to have anything signed. I just wanted the Trial Chamber to see this salamander and also the distribution of the villages. If that is the reason, then we can have this admitted, this section of the map, that is, without having it signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has this not been admitted previously?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D225, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the whole map, but I meant this segment of Srebrenica and Bratunac. But all right. The Trial Chamber can always have it enlarged when they need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, with the magic of e-court we can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We don't need the map anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said in several places that you had attended a meeting at the cinema, where Mr. Miroslav Deronjic, president of the SDS of Bratunac, said -- and I'm going to quote that and I'm going to say what the paragraph is, and that is 16, let me not say anything more than that, paragraph 16 of the amalgamated statement. You say that he said: "If there have to be conflicts, if conflicts break out in Bosnia, then we are going to do our best to ensure that Bratunac is the last place where this will happen." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the conflict in Bosnia broke out on the 26th of March in Brod, on the 31st of March in Bijeljina, on the 2nd and 3rd of April at Kupres, and in Bratunac, it was only sometime in May?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I don't know about the other conflicts. I wouldn't know what the answers would be. But in Bratunac, the conflict broke out a lot earlier. Actually, there were conflicts, there were killings that started a lot earlier, barricades, misunderstandings. But true ethnic cleansing and persecutions started around the 9th of May, and then on the 10th of May my neighbourhood had its inhabitants expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to that. When I ask you about dates, then let us identify the dates. Let us not go any further than that ethnic cleansing, et cetera. That is a particular qualification and then I have to do more than is necessary. Tell us, please, are you referring to barricades, crises, and killings that occurred in 1991?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, yes, that happened as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you preserved the peace until the 9th of May, if we make an exception in the case of what happened in September 1991, when there was this killing in Kravica and the barricades were there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, for all of four weeks you had peace, four weeks longer than the rest of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how you can call that peace. People were afraid. People were detained. People did not move around. We did not dare go into town. What kind of peace was that? I don't know what was going on elsewhere. Quite simply, there was fear, we were expecting something to happen, and then what happened did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say people were detained, you mean that they shut themselves up? It's not that somebody else had detained them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, yes. People were shut in their homes and yards, and some people would walk out and say that the situation was not good, that there are some armies there and that there are weapons there and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd ask Your Honours to consider redacting from line 24 on page 26 to 27, line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm going to call this "your village," and I am kindly asking you not to mention its name. Can you tell me, why did you ask for protective measures to be granted to you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, I asked for protective measures for one single reason: I wanted to provide protection for my family. After my first (redacted) I had serious problems. There were threats made, people called me anonymously on the phone, and I had all sorts of problems and the local authorities are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I might agree that only victims are entitled to protective measures, not witnesses, but that was a decision of the Chamber and I'm not interested in your motives. In your amalgamated statement, did you say in paragraph 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was an unnecessary and improper comment during the course of your examination. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and I'm sorry to keep doing this, but I'd like to redact line -- the first word in 28, line 6.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Excellency, but I have no other way of indicating and showing to you that I have 142 witnesses of which only two are viva voce witnesses. And there's a plethora of protective measures that, in my mind, are totally unnecessary. So this proceedings look to me to be somewhat odd. I don't want some untruths to be discovered by people on the ground because I am receiving feedback information that untruths are being spoken here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I meant, Mr. Karadzic, was this is not a proper moment, i.e., in the presence of the witness, to argue as to the appropriateness of protective measures. Let's move on. And the word to be redacted is not your words, it's ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will take care to refer to his village as a village only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 20 of your amalgamated statement, did you say that first a JNA officer arrived and that he wanted to collect the military records. Since he was denied that, he came again with some people, but the residents prevented him from taking these records and that you took part in that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you said that after this incident, all Muslims and other non-Serbs refused to respond to mobilisation and refused to participate in the war in Croatia. Up until the 31st of August, had the Muslims went to do their military service and responded to call-ups and stopped doing that after the 31st of August?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I don't know if I can answer that because I was not in the government structure in the municipality and I did not keep record of who went and who didn't. Anyway, I heard that there were people who refused to join the army and to be mobilised and sent away to a front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear that much earlier Mr. Izetbegovic and the Muslim and Croatian part of the Presidency had recommended that conscripts refused to respond to mandatory, compulsory military service or mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, I personally didn't hear that, but people used to talk about that, the people of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then this sentence where you said that after that incident the Muslims and Serbs refused to respond wouldn't be correct; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 22, you said - and I'm paraphrasing in Serbian - that paramilitary groups started appearing in Bratunac on the 17th of April. You said that there were Arkan's and Seselj's troops. They used to drive cars belonging to the Yugoslav People's Army. They were dressed in camouflage uniforms, et cetera. Can you tell me, please, the reservists who responded to mobilisation call-ups, what kind of uniforms did they have and what kind of vehicles did they drive in?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, the reservists who responded to the mobilisation were mostly Serbs. And since what was all -- it was already summer, they were dressed in summer uniforms, military uniforms. As for the vehicles in -- if there was any movement of troops, they would normally use army vehicles, but I don't remember that there was much movement initially, after the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that these people there were Arkan's formations and you say that they declared themselves as belonging to Arkan's or Seselj's formations? How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have information from a worker who used to work with me. I was his foreman. He left his job very early, he told me that he was going to Croatia to the battle-field. And after a month or two, after that, I saw him again in Bratunac. I saw him in town. And he told me that he was a member of Arkan's unit that was fighting in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have to go into closed session once I decide to ask you to tell me his name. Here you say that you were told this by your Serbian neighbours and also I will ask you their names in a closed session. But tell me, how do you know that there were Seselj's men there as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: The majority of information we got was from the people who went into town as well as the Serbs with whom we still had some contacts, those were the citizens that retained their jobs and their Serb friends told them that Arkan's men and Seselj's men were coming, that they wanted to cause disruption, and that we were going to drive them out and that we would not allow them to create problems in our town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But judging by the insignia, it was impossible for you to determine who was which paramilitary unit in particular. Were you able to recognise who the JNA reservists were?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, because I knew almost everybody in Bratunac, not by name but by sight, and I saw a lot of local Serbs who put on those military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph, you say that you heard many things from other Bosnians who at that time, in mid-April, were still going to work alongside their Serbian neighbours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this Bane came from and to which unit did he belong?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Bane said that he was from Serbia, that he was a member of Arkan's unit, and we-- quite simply, he said that he had been invited to come there, that he had been paid to kill people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will come to this issue of payment. You inquired about this with the local Serbs, but can you tell me when did that man have this cross carved in his arm?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: This cross was carved, in my opinion, on the second day inside the hall. They brought school desks and put them in a circle in the middle of the hall. That is when Bane and the other two men who killed most people would call people's names. But sometimes even if you established an eye contact with this Bane, he would simply point a finger at you and say: Come out, and you would have to come inside the circle. Sometimes they would take a volleyball ball and hurl it at somebody, and the detainee that he hit with the ball was forced to come into that circle, where he was beaten and some people were beaten to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that was on the second day. When was that? So you said you came to this school on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I was brought to this school on two occasions. The first time I was singled out from a column that was supposed to enter the stadium. They simply told me that I couldn't go in, that I had to make a statement. They took me to the school building where they beat me. A Serb friend of mine recognised me, tried to rescue me so that I wouldn't be killed, but I cannot relocate you. You will have to go to the stadium again and then you will be transported to Tuzla. I was returned to the stadium, and when -- in early evening they started evacuating people from the stadium --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Let us just identify the day when this man had this cross carved in his arm.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether that happened on the first or the second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 11th/12th?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: The 12th or the 13th. Everything that happened in the hall in Bratunac happened on those two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 12th or 13th of May. You arrived in Visoko on the 17th of May?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was either the 17th or the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation how -- as to how it was possible for this wound to heal so quickly and that completely new skin, fresh skin, emerged?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not an expert. People were injured in all sorts of ways from the beating. When -- if they beating someone and they decided to kill someone, they would leave the one who was being beaten and then go away and then we would try to help this person. As for this wound, I don't know how long it took for it to heal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am a physician. What it looks to me, Mr. Witness, is as if something was rubbed in, into the skin. If it had really been the skin carved with a knife, four days is not enough for such heal -- wound to heal.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: You're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. Karadzic, you are giving evidence. That is simply not permissible and this is not an expert witness. He can't deal with it, but there are other ways that you can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Further, the witness has answered the question. Let us move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today, on page 9, you said that your name was called out -- some people were called out as well to come out to be beaten. And elsewhere you said -- and I can find the exact reference. You said that sometimes they called the names of the people who weren't there at all. Can you decide in what way and what criterion did they apply in calling out your names? Why did they call your names at all? Why didn't they take you out one by one?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, I personally believe that pieces of paper were being brought from another room. Somebody would bring it to the door and the guard would then pass these people on to those who were doing the killings, and before that, they would call out the names. That happened on a number of occasions, and I think that that happened to people who had some dispute with a Serb or an altercation or a fight. That was a good chance to exact revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 32 you say that you had not seen the killing of Mumin Selimovic and that you heard most of these things. In paragraph 33, the last sentence says: [In English] "I did not witness it myself." [Interpretation] So you say that you did not witness it yourself. Can we ask you to identify all the things that you heard and to make a distinction between that and the things that you saw. What was it that you saw? Did you see that cross being carved into that arm? A few moments ago, you said that you did see that.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I did see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And blood came out then?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I think there was blood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where in paragraph 32 - could Dr. Karadzic show me - the witness said that he heard most of these things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here it is in paragraph 32: [In English] "On 18th of April, 1992, a local salesman called Mumin Selimovic was killed. He was found dead by the Krizevica River. I knew Mumin Selimovic well. He was the manager of the department store in Bratunac, so everybody in Bratunac knew him. I did not see it, but I only heard from people detained with him," or with me, probably, because it is obviously partially [indiscernible] --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, there was no problem reading that part out, that he heard about this incident, but Mr. Karadzic tried to imply that the witness had somewhere said that he heard most of these things, and that's nowhere in the paragraph he cited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in paragraph 33, as well, at the end, it says: "I did not witness it myself." I did not see this personally. But with regard to most incidents -- actually, the witness heard about more things than he saw, but about the carving of the cross in the arm, blood gushes out, in that case. And that is what we would like to hear about. It is different when it is carved in with a knife or if something else happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you saw that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And there was blood?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, you cannot say that it exactly gushed, but since this was an army knife, experts know full well that it is not sharp, it is just a pointed knife, and it can leave a strong mark, but it does not necessarily mean that there has to be lots of blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the skin cut?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I think it had been cut, but not very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now we'll take the break for 25 minutes and resume at ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with these events in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know which events I'm being asked about. I knew about most of the incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on the 9th of April there was an agreement reached that the public security station would be divided and that there would be a Serb part and a Muslim part, and that they remained on the same premises but on different floors?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, I know that there was a separation, but what the agreement was exactly, I don't know, and they were not in the same building, but, rather, in two different buildings. The Bosnian police remained in the old police station, whereas the Serb policemen who opted for the Serbian police left and were located in an old school building not far from the train station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you confirmed this when you said that on the 18th of April some volunteers arrived, some of whom joined paramilitary groups and others joined the JNA as volunteers; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, these volunteers arrived. They had -- they came from Serbia. That was the information that I had. And a group of them took lodging at Fontana Hotel in Bratunac. Later on, they had a headquarters in cafe called Jasen, which was not far from the church and mosque in Bratunac, because in Bratunac, I believe the church and the mosque actually were on the same plot of land. They were on either side of a road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it correct that the Serbs and Muslims -- the leadership, the Serbian and Muslim leadership, had joint meetings with these volunteers at Hotel Fontana? Just tell us if you know about it.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, I did hear that there was a meeting, and I also heard from a Bosniak who had come from Tuzla who told me that these volunteers told them that they should leave there for Tuzla, they should go back to Tuzla, and they did. He didn't say why he had to go, but he said that he was trying to save his skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's try and make a distinction between paramilitaries and volunteers. I'm sure that you could see for yourself that this Bane was an Arkan man, but, as for the others, you couldn't really make the distinction?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, yes, Bane said that he was an Arkan man. He didn't have any insignia. He had just a uniform that was sort of nondescript. Everyone had uniforms like that. Others had other uniforms, and they, themselves, said that they were Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the local reservists had JNA uniforms and insignia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, yes. The locals - and there were quite a few of them - had JNA uniforms and of course they bore JNA insignia. But some didn't even have any insignia but just the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Naser Oric set an ambush on the 20th of April for these volunteers, on which occasion he killed 12 of these volunteers and disposed of their bodies by dumping them in the river?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, all I can say is that I heard information -- I heard the -- about these things. I didn't see anything for myself -- with my own eyes. I was at home at the time. I heard that these -- that this Arkan group of volunteers had come to Srebrenica. I did see them riding around town in some vehicles and looting, and they went to the local department store where they looted some items. And most probably what happened was that on their way back this ambush was set up, or maybe they had gone back and then returned, and on that occasion they were ambushed. But he didn't really throw their bodies into the river. He just set up this ambush. What happened was that some of them got killed, and as the river ran nearby, I heard later on that some of their bodies were actually recovered from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, did this actually contribute to a deterioration of the relationship between Srebrenica and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The situation in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Serbian public security station --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I want to tell you to put a pause. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that you heard that the situation in Bratunac was exacerbated by this, but you did not see this for yourself. But you could actually see for yourself that the tensions had risen?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did. You could feel it. And especially when we heard of this incident, then we also got frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Serbian public security station had only 11 police officers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know how many police officers there were from the time when the police separated. I never went into the police station anymore and I didn't have any contacts with anyone from either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that these paramilitaries were a dominant force there, that they confiscated police vehicles from the police officers and that they began to enforce the law there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't tell you what they did or what happened, but the fact is that we heard the screeching and sirens of police vehicles. These vehicles were from another state and you could hear this at night. Of course this was totally unusual. We heard the sirens of police vehicles. We heard them crossing the bridge. And we concluded that something was wrong and that the situation in the town itself was very bad, so we did not go there anymore. We never ventured out of our homes after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in late April, is it correct that another group of volunteers arrived and that they, too, split, that one group joined the JNA, and the others as volunteers, and the others just formed a paramilitary group. So did this paramilitary force that was there, was it reinforced by this new group?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know much about that. I did hear that there was another group that arrived. I don't know exactly when it was, I just heard that there was a group of paramilitaries at the Fontana Hotel and there was another group at the Jasen cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that on the 3rd of May in Hranca, which is between a Serbian village and Glogova, a JNA column was attacked in which 12 men -- and in this attack 12 men were killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were never told, nor did I ever hear that a column was attacked, and especially not that there were 12 fatalities of 12 dead Serbian soldiers. I did hear on one occasion from an old man, the father of Ismet, the cobbler, who was -- that there was a man brought from Hranca, a very old man, whose back was -- who had a hump on his back. And this man was brought into the room and was beaten by this Bane. He was the one who said that there was a column going through Hranca. And then Bane said: Well, this column was attacked while it was going through Hranca and you contributed to this, and so on, and this poor man said: How could I have done anything? Look at me, I'm an old man. And, anyhow, I think that he was killed, that Bane shot at him and he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You think he was killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, yes, I know that he was killed at the hangar. I am sure that you can actually easily establish that because there were quite a few men who were killed there and who were then buried at the Bratunac cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the 8th of May, Goran Zekic, a deputy and judge, was killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's correct. I'm sure it is true. I heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that following these two incidents the road between Kravica and Rogova --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And Glogova, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- was cut off, that barricades or roadblocks were erected there and that this only contributed to a further deterioration?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, that's possible but I never took that road. I did not go towards Glogova and I can't really tell. But I do know that Goran Zekic was killed. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: (redacted) And that's how I heard, but I didn't take that road again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That means that you don't know who took part in the incident on the 9th of May in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. Nicholls is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. Could we go into private session for one second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You described how your village and Mihajlovic and Krasan Polje were places where paramilitaries came, or volunteers, but I think you also mentioned that the JNA entered the villages, or its volunteers, and demanded that weapons be surrendered because then they -- their security and safety could be guaranteed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The army came and they asked for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Milutin Milosevic prevented the rape of a young girl, beat up a member of this paramilitary group?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that I've heard of this particular incident, but I did hear of occasions where crimes were prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that as a result of all these incidents -- we've seen that there was a killing on the 20th of April by Arkan's men or other paramilitaries; then the 3rd May, the attack on the column; the 8th of May, the murder of Goran Zekic. Is it correct that then a lynch mob was -- came into being, as it were, and that it became very dangerous for Muslims to move around and that that's why it was dangerous to, for instance, go to the health centre, and so on?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, certainly it was dangerous, especially because we, Muslims, had no leadership. We didn't have any organised group of people who would advise us on what to do. We were just left to our own devices. We were just sitting there waiting for God knows what to happen. We signed our oaths of allegiance to the Serbian municipality. Some people returned who had earlier left for Tuzla, but I just want to say that before the murder of Goran Zekic -- before the killing of Goran Zekic and these people in Potocari, there had been the attack on Srebrenica, where there was a lot of shooting and shelling. There were helicopters flying over, going to Srebrenica, so that the overall situation was laden with fear and difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you were not in Srebrenica, were you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that your leadership, as early as mid-April, left Bratunac, or part of your Muslim leadership?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Most of our leaders simply left. They just -- the authorities just sort of fell apart. They were afraid. They realised they couldn't do anything there, so they just left because we were exposed. You could see on the other side of the Drina you could see the Serbs or they could see us. And simply Nijaz Durakovic told me one day: Well, don't worry, if need be, we will just move out. We will hand the town over to them. If need be, we will provide transportation for all of you. But anyhow, whether they voluntarily or not, in any case, we tried to save our skins.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You speak about that in paragraph 36 of your statement, that between the 18th and 29th of April, the ultimatum period, you say that it was relatively peaceful, and you say that: We were asked to return to work and allowed to move freely in town. And then you say: Most of the Muslim population had left the area over the next few weeks. Many did not return to work because they were too afraid. That is what you are saying; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who called you back to work? Who asked the refugees to come back? Who called the Muslims to go back to work?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: For the most part, these were individual calls, people who happened to have some contact with Serbs. And then they talked about it in town. They said that the Serbs took over the government in town and all of that was happening, and they were saying that they as the authorities, the government, and the Serb police were providing guarantees. Some people believed that. They went back to work. This did not last for a very long time. I personally did not leave home at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you about the number of policemen. How many houses and apartments were abandoned when this population left in mid-April? How many houses had to be guarded? Many, right, many?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, quite a few Bosniak houses were in town, in the centre of town. I don't know how many policemen there were. At any rate, people left their homes in the centre of town and most of the people who lived outside the centre did not leave their houses. However, some people from the centre of town did not flee to Tuzla either. They simply spent their time in the suburbs, or rather, these places that were further away from town, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 37 you say that -- I'm going to read it out in English: [In English] "The Serbs made it appear as if they wanted the people back and everything was back to normal." [Interpretation] The last sentence of this paragraph [as interpreted]: [In English] "... Bratunac municipality, that we are signing this --" Ah-ha: "I cannot give you exact wording, but the main thing I remember about the content of these papers was that it said we were loyal citizens of the Bratunac municipality, that we are signing this document, and in exchange for this signature, they are going to guarantee the safety of our property and our freedom." [Interpretation] Does that mean that if you live in your own house, and if you state that you're not going to shoot, they, on their part, will guarantee your security?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: We signed an oath of allegiance to that municipality; quite simply, we had no choice. That is what we were told when signing this and also during some contacts. However, there was very little contact, because we were afraid when we came before the municipality and when we were signing this. We said that the precondition was that, that is to say, whoever does not sign this will not have a security guarantee. And practically all of us decided to do it, all of us from my neighbourhood went there and signed that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 41, you describe that, as for your village -- no, settlement - it's not a village - an officer came there. He assembled you there, Remzija Halilovic did, and the officer delivered a speech, said that he was a captain of the JNA and that he was in charge of the security of the civilian population of Bratunac. He proposed that you hand over your weapons. He said that it was up to you; however, he thought that it would be better for you to surrender your weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When all of this happened, when all of these people were killed, and when this lynch atmosphere came into being, you say that you were told to assemble at the stadium for the sake of your own safety. Do you agree that 11 Serb policemen could not protect even themselves, let alone masses of people like that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, our very own neighbours, the locals, took us from our homes and brought us there. I had no way of knowing there were only 11 Serb policemen there. There were a lot of people in Bratunac who were armed. These volunteers did not really go out of town to get people. I remember that morning when we were picked up, there was such a lot of gun-fire around town that I thought it was perhaps 2 kilometres away from my house. I thought the shooting was right underneath my window. And I saw everything in flames, hills, sheds where the cattle were, everything. I fled from home. I told my wife that I had to run away. After that, I saw men in military uniforms getting close to the houses, and all of a sudden people were on the road leading to town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 46, you say that you thought it was time for you to hide, and you told your wife to watch the children. So you left your children to your wife and your wife to your children because they were not in danger. Otherwise, you, as a traditional Balkan male, would not have done that. Why would you have to hide as opposed to them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that this question is really -- well, we all knew that the military-aged men were the first to be detained and arrested and that they would leave women and children alone. I did not hide very far away from my home. I couldn't go very far away. I just went to some bushes about 200 metres away from my house, and I observed the situation. At the moment when a man came to us and said that our family members were under threat, as the gentleman said just now, when I realised, as a Bosnian male, that my family would be in danger, I left the bushes and joined my family in this column.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible, though, that the army held something against you or some paramilitaries did? Because you see here that in August 1991, you took part in this operation that prevented the army from carrying out its duties related to military files? Also, your brother had deserted in 1991 from the JNA, as an active-duty military officer, and came to live with you. Was that perhaps the reason why you had to hide and your family did not have to hide?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: That's not the reason. Quite simply, atmosphere was like that. We, all the men, thought that we should hide a bit. We knew that there was no place to hide, but anyway. It's not that anyone had anything against me, either the soldiers or anybody else in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it is correct that you did prevent the army from taking military files and that your brother deserted in 1991 and came to live with you; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in paragraph 48, did you say that you had been told to seek shelter at this stadium for your own protection? Is that true or not? And were you told that you would be protected from Arkan's men there, Arkan's men who were causing all the problems; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, when leaving the houses, and when I left the bushes and when I got out into the road that leads to town - and then, later on, from town to the stadium - along the way people had some contact with these soldiers and what was said was that they would simply take us to the stadium, protect us, prevent Arkan's men from killing us and robbing us, and a few people from my neighbourhood should give statements and then we would all be allowed to go home. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the reason why you thought that the moment of your arrest was not when you came out with your family but the moment when you were taken from the stadium to the station to give an interview or statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, I heard, Your Honours, that these guards were reading out my name on the road in connection with two other people from (redacted) who were supposed to give statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you were taken to the station. First, you hid in the bushes, then you joined your family, then you set out to the stadium, as instructed. And along the way to the stadium, you were told that you should go to the station to give a statement; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: As we were about to get to the main road, I was recognised by one of my employees, previous employees. He walked up to me and said, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: (redacted) As we were getting closer to the stadium, two soldiers walked up to me and asked me whether I was such and such a person and I was told that I had to go to the police station to give a statement. And that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Occasionally, you said that your suburb, or your neighbourhood, had up to 3.000 inhabitants including women and children; is that right? However, there were fewer than 1.000 of them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are going back to the same question again. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: (redacted) proper itself, then the number of inhabitants is lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Something has to be redacted, obviously, and the Defence has no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Branko Jovanovic wanted a list to be made of the Muslims who were issued weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If necessary, we can go into private session for a short time. Do we need a private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they get this list that they wanted, and how long was it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I did not make any list. I simply told them that I didn't distribute any weapons, that I, myself, didn't have any weapon, that I hadn't been making any lists. That enraged them, and they said, "All right. Let's go to the hall and you're going to see us killing." And they simply said that that will happen to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true - and I can refer you to proofing notes (redacted) - that you said that the Serbs told the local Serb authorities that they were fighting the paramilitaries with the aim of chasing them out of the zone but that they were not exactly successful in that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, some Serbs used to say that. I could never believe that was true, that they couldn't manage to deal with a group of people. But we did hear that from our Serb acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is contained in 1D4113. You also said in that same statement, in that same document, rather, that the guards told you that everything was going to be all right as soon as the Serbian leadership managed to expel those people outside the town and that neither you nor they knew who was paying them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. While these killers were passing from the hall, the guards at the door who were our neighbours were very kind and polite. They talked to us and they told us, "Okay, you who remained here, we are going to try and save you. Don't be afraid. The only problem we have to resolve is to get rid of Arkan's men, and you will be released after that." We believed that that was a good plan, and we expected that to come true. However, an officer came into the hall and, quite simply, he started shouting, "What are you doing with these people?" And with the simple command, he just drove all these people out of the hall and they left after a few hours. This officer then brought some food and water, together with two soldiers. But as soon as he went away, these same people reappeared and continued the killing. So I really couldn't understand what was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say in your statement given to the (redacted) (redacted) that you noticed that people were singled out according to a certain pattern, and that people from Potocari were in greater danger because the group of Arkan's was killed -- Arkan's men were killed there? It's document 1D142. Did -- is that what you observed, that these people were in greater dangers and that they were more frequently singled out?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's what I observed. I heard them asking several times whether there were people from Potocari or Srebrenica, and anyone who responded was severely beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt, at page 53, line 8, could we redact the date. I haven't come up with it until now. I just wanted to check in the prior testimony he has referred to by exactly the same date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Actually, the transcript does not contain the date, actually. Did --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Our transcript, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It does on page 53, line 8, to the proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The month was not reflected. I am -- very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, it didn't -- I think it was said but did not show up in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was not translated. I remember that. But in any event, we will delete it, redact it. Yes. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the area of Potocari the place where on or around the 20th of April, 12 Arkan's men were killed, and was it also the area where Judge Zekic was killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The area of Potocari, as I heard, was the location where this fighting took place; however, how many people were killed and who was killed, I don't know. I just heard that some Arkan men were killed and that there were casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On page 54, Your Honour, for the same reasons, lines 9 and 10, refers to the date of the statement and the ERN, and that statement was an exhibit in the prior case, a public exhibit, under 89(F), I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Isn't that under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not in the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're not quite sure -- you were not quite sure whose bodies you saw in relation to the hangar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: While entering the hangar, I couldn't distinguish any bodies. The only body I saw was one body that I saw when I was taken to the school for the second time. That was the body of a neighbour of mine who was killed there and when he was thrown into the lavatory that was in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true - and we're not going to mention any family members of Judge Zekic - that they were going to find out who was responsible for his death and that he would be revenged?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I believe that that person came to the hall and he asked who had killed his son. He said, "I'm really sorry, but 300 of you will have to pay for the death of my son."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that somewhere Dzemo Hodzic, an employee from Osijek, an employee from the draft office and a reserve captain, was beaten up and put on the truck together with the dead bodies. He was alive and he was shouting, "Brothers, run away, you are going to be killed"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Has this been recorded? Has this been investigated? Is there any investigation, related material?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if this was recorded. We heard his voice. We heard it coming from outside. And later on, people told us that that man was on board the truck. Some people were shouting and he was taken back to the hall. He was so badly beaten that he died as a result, and then his body was taken out. I don't know whether to the hangar or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you heard that from the outside?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, because the windows were open and we could hear that voice behind the hall and under the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Is it true that you were told that they couldn't protect you until they cleansed Bratunac from all paramilitary and that that was the reason for you being taken to Pale?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we were in the hall, nobody told us that they couldn't protect us from the paramilitary. The only thing that they told us was when we were being taken out of the village, some of our uniformed neighbours told us that there was a misunderstanding with the Arkan's men, and that they would like to have us all in one place in order to provide better protection. However, what was the background of all of that, I don't know, and I invite everyone to draw their own conclusions as they please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then on the 13th of May, was it the 13th of May or which date, you were taken to the sports hall in Pale?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it was late in the evening. I don't remember. It might have been around midnight. Soldiers entered the hall and told us, "You are going to Pale. Lorries are coming. You are safe now. Act correctly, don't try to escape, don't risk your lives. You are going to Pale to be exchanged." And that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that at Pale you didn't see anyone being killed and that the policemen did not allow any soldiers to enter the premises where the detainees were. That's what you stated; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, and, if necessary, I can describe the situation. We were just sometimes smacked on our way to the lavatory or maybe kicked, but nothing major, no major beatings. We saw that there were bars on the doors and the policemen were standing at the door. Whoever came to the door, if he was a soldier, he would be prevented from entering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In another statement, or rather, (redacted) you said that the army tried to establish some law and order -- intervened. This does not pertain to Pale. It was before that, to establish some kind of order and to intervene; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I do not remember that. Maybe I did state that somewhere. Perhaps that is what some Serbs had told us, that the army was trying to establish some order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
