utterances.text: All right. Let us not go into closed session. I don't want us to waste time. So, then, together with these 400 persons in Pale and 400 persons in Visoko -- so, the number of people who set out, returned as well. You crossed over to the Muslim side. You called that an exchange. Who crossed over to the Serb side from the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know who crossed over. Once, while we were in Pale, perhaps a day before the exchange, or perhaps two days before that, but I think it was just one day, a soldier appeared at the door screaming. I think he actually wanted to get in. He was shouting and saying that if his brother who was captured in Sarajevo would be killed, that he would kill all of us, that we should all pray for his life; otherwise, we will not stay alive. So we came to that conclusion. No one told us who we would be exchanged for. We came to the conclusion that this exchange would take place and we were praying and hoping that all of that took place in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that they had to protect you from the enraged people when you were boarding the buses. People were furious. It wasn't only one soldier but there were lots of people who were very angry at you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honours. We were not on buses. We were transported from Pale in open trucks, that is to say, with no cover. And we were tied by ropes, ten by ten of us. And the last, tenth, person would be tied to the truck. From the buildings around us and from the terraces there and also the masses of people who were around us, they were throwing stones. A friend of mine next to me was hit by a can that made his head bleed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for what the guards were telling you about the attempts of the Serb leaders to get soldiers out, you spoke about that in page -- in paragraph 77. I'm just saying that for the benefit of the participants so that they know what I'm referring to. So you're sure that 400 people left Pale and came to their destination. How many people were there who were so enraged? Why were they so enraged? Did some of their nearest and dearest get killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I don't know why people were enraged. I have no information about any casualties in Pale. I just know that in Pale, as we entered the hall, all of us from Bratunac were basically sitting on the floor. And on the left-hand side, there were wooden benches. And on these wooden benches, there were some other people. Later on, we found out when we had some contact, they said that they were Muslims and that they were captured around Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Several times you kindly corrected yourself. You said that you had heard that some people had been killed, but it would be invaluable if you could tell us the names of these individuals. Did you know Bajro Mahmutovic, the son of Sinahim [phoen] Mahmutovic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Bajro Mahmutovic? I never mentioned him. I don't know. I don't remember. There are quite a few Mahmutovics. But, Bajro, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. He's from Zanjevo. You don't know his son. You don't know how he lost his life. You didn't hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Then we're not going to go into that. So you were brought to Semizovac -- or, rather, to the border, to the front line between the Serb and Muslim forces near Visoko; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Your Honours. We stopped briefly at a particular place where there were Serbs. I think it was called Ilijas. There was some misunderstanding there, too. There were some verbal attacks by civilians against our trucks. Since these were open trucks, we heard the soldiers, the Serb soldiers, shouting that the border, the separation line was closed. At one moment I even heard one of their superiors tell them, "If there is a skirmish, try to fire single gun-shots and economise with your ammunition."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is as you were getting closer to the border; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then the separation line was crossed. The Serb lines were crossed, and then the Muslim lines were crossed. Who mediated in this entire effort and who facilitated it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: On the Serb side, it was the army. And when we entered the peaceful area where we no longer heard the citizens, and, quite simply, we didn't hear anybody or anything anymore, we were outside populated areas, we were at a clearing, we were stopped there. I think I was in the first truck. The trucks were open and I saw soldiers of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is what their emblem said, TO. They walked up to us and said that we should be careful, that we were saved. They gave us some knives. They started cutting the rope. We started getting off the trucks. And one by one, we walked in the direction that we were told to go into for about 100 metres or so. We kept on walking and we saw a lot of civilian vehicles, buses that transported us to a hall in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Nevertheless, Serb trucks did not cross Muslim lines. You stopped on no man's land before the Muslim lines. That's where the trucks stopped?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be sure and say where we were exactly. Quite simply, when the trucks stopped we heard people speaking outside. When they opened the truck for us, we saw Serb soldiers and a few TO BH soldiers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So there was no incident involved, nobody opened fire or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: That is correct, there was no incident there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you were put up at this hall in Visoko. Is that a sports hall or what?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: It's an enormous hall out of town. It was a sports hall and there were still some flags outside. There was the Yugoslav flag. So we knew that it was a sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that where they made lists, where they wrote all of your names, and does that list correspond to the list that was compiled in Pale, and were there exactly 400 of you on those lists?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: They wrote down our names there. Of course we were checked, examined, assisted. I don't know what the list from Pale was, and I don't know whether these two lists correspond to each other. I don't know whether they coincide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then how long did you stay in the hall? How long did you stay and how long did the others stay?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I was in the hall for a while. I could not stand on my feet. I asked for medical assistance. Doctors came. They tried to help me, quite simply. My back was painful, my kidneys. I was taken to an infirmary. They tried to alleviate the pain. All of that was in vain for about two or three hours -- two or three days, and then they decided to transport me to the medical centre of Zenica, to the hospital there. But they also said that there were some difficulties involved because we'd have to cross an area that was held by Serbs, Serb lines, Serb roadblocks, and it was for me to decide. And I could no longer take the pain and I said, "I'm going no matter what."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, are you coming to an end? How long do you need?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as you say, Excellency, whatever you say. Perhaps a few more questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: See if you could conclude in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So did you cross these barricades and were you in an ambulance?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Yes, I was in an ambulance. I passed these barricades. I had Red Cross papers on me stating that I had been exchanged, and they told me that if anybody at the roadblock says anything, that I should just keep silent, that I should say that I was exchanged, and that's the way that it was. I think we stopped by the roadblock, they looked at that piece of paper, and they let me go to Zenica, to the hospital there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this a Serb officer or an ordinary soldier?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: A Serb police manned these barricades, roadblocks, they wore Serb police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the rest, do you know how long they stayed on in that hall in Visoko?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I think that these people stayed on for about a month. Others stayed even longer in Visoko. I was in Zenica for a while. I heard that my wife was in trouble in Tuzla, that she was at this school with our children. We spoke on the telephone. She said that there wasn't enough food, that it was very difficult. The doctors advised that I stayed in the hospital longer. I heard that a relative of mine from Visoko was prepared to go to Tuzla. And I asked the doctors to allow me to go and spend the weekend in Visoko so that I would contact my relative and say hello to my wife and children. I came to Visoko. When I was actually supposed to go to Visoko there were no longer any roadblocks there. Quite simply, the Bosnians took that area and the roadblocks, too. I came to Visoko and I decided to walk to Tuzla together with my relative and a group of people, and that is how we tried to get there. Sometimes we got some transportation, like trucks, and in other places we didn't. But we ultimately reached Tuzla after a night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that your countrymen who remained in Visoko returned towards Sarajevo, joined the unit in Ahatovici and many of them were captured yet again, once again? Did anyone tell you about that, what the fate of the others was; that is to say that they were captured yet again, taken prisoner once again, these very same people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: I had not heard of that, that they were taken prisoner again. How do I put this? The partner of a relative of mine said that he saw his wife and children being killed, and then he joined the TO in Visoko and set out towards Sarajevo, and I heard that he lost his life during that breakthrough. As for taking people prisoner, Your Honours, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you join the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina at a particular point in time after leaving Zenica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: After arriving in Tuzla sometime in the autumn, late in the autumn, I joined the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Perhaps at that time it was called the army or was it still the TO? No one forced me to do that. However, all of those people who joined in received food packages and money, and since there was hunger in Tuzla, I volunteered to go. I left that food and some money to my wife and children. I was mobilised thereby. I was trained for a while. Then I was on guard duty in Teocak. That was very brief. There was no fighting up there, no operations, no shooting, just a bit of sporadic gun-fire. I received a telegram from my command that my wife was very ill, that she had to undergo heart surgery. I went back to Tuzla. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last question, Witness, I don't have enough time to show all these documents and perhaps you won't know much about some of them. My last question is as follows: When you got off the Serb bus -- Serb trucks near Visoko, were some Serbs loaded onto these trucks, or, rather, did you see any Serbs crossing from the Muslim side to the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, I could not see anything. Actually, I did not see anything. I didn't express any interest. As soon as I got off the truck, I was told that I should go straight ahead. I walked down that road straight ahead. I couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that someone had told the people there that: If you respect the president and the state, this convoy would be allowed to pass through. If you respect your president and your state, you will allow this convoy to get through?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not remember having heard that and I do not know who it was who said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Thank you for your testimony and please don't hold anything against me.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-605
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could redact, please, line 65, 13, at the end, to 17. It's, again, a relatively unique little segment that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- explained before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, your testimony has now come to an end. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go, but we will rise all together. We'll take a break for 25 minutes and resume at ten to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Edgerton. Before we begin to hear the evidence of the next witness, his evidence, there are a few matters to deal with. Let me see. First of all, the Chamber is seized of the accused's motion for eighth suspension of proceedings: Witness KDZ-490 filed on 23rd of August, 2011, and the Prosecution's response to that motion filed today. While, in the Chamber's decision on accused's motion for modification of protective measures, Witnesses KDZ-490 and KDZ-492 dated 25th of March, 2010, the Chamber was satisfied that delayed disclosure of KDZ-490's identity until 21 days prior to the witness's testimony was justified. The Chamber acknowledges that the accused will require additional time to consider the volume of Rule 66(A)(ii) material disclosed with respect to the delayed disclosure Witness KDZ-490. However, the Chamber is not convinced that a suspension of proceedings is necessary to allow the accused and his team to complete this review. The material can be reviewed on a rolling basis and any material the accused and his team have been unable to consider can be reviewed during the scheduled break in proceedings from 10th of October to 14th of October, 2011. Further, the Chamber does not consider that calling the witness after 17th of October, 2011, would adversely impact on the protective measure of delayed disclosure granted to him. The Chamber therefore denies the motion but instructs the Prosecution not to call the witness, KDZ-490, before 17th of October, 2011. Then I will deal with two matters emanating from yesterday's hearing. Firstly, the Chamber refers to Mr. Robinson's motion made during yesterday's hearing to strike out para 12 of Mr. Gusic's amalgamated statement which bears exhibit number P3196. Having heard the parties, the Chamber is satisfied that the additional evidence provided yesterday by the witness in relation to paragraph 12 provides sufficient clarification to the information therein, and, therefore, that the exclusion of paragraph 12 is not warranted. The request is, therefore, denied. However, in this regard the Chamber notes that, as with all determinations of admissibility, the weight and probative value, if any, of any admitted evidence falls to be assessed when the evidence has been heard in its totality. Secondly, with respect to the admissibility of 1D4092, the Chamber notes that, except for the cover page, it is not a document produced by a member of the European Parliament; rather, it is a "dossier" compiling information on crimes against Serbs gathered by two individuals, Stojsavljevic and Gerratt. The witness was shown a few pages of the document, including the one where his name appears. However, he did not provide much information about his position on the contents of the document. As such, the Chamber will not admit the document. Finally, the Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's request for leave to add documents to the 65 ter list, filed on 2nd of August, 2011, as part of its 92 ter notification of submission of written evidence for Witness KDZ-033. The Chamber has reviewed each of the documents and finds that each is relevant and of sufficient importance to justify their late addition to the 65 ter exhibit list. Additionally, because each is indispensable and inseparable from KDZ-033's amalgamated witness statement, the Chamber finds that the Prosecution has shown good cause for its request. Finally, the Chamber notes that the accused did not respond to the request and the Chamber is satisfied that the amendments at this stage of the proceedings provide the accused sufficient notice and do not adversely affect his ability to prepare for trial. The Chamber thus grants leave for the Prosecution to add Rule 65 ter numbers 23197 to 23209, 23211 to 23218, 23221, and 23222 to its 65 ter exhibit list. Unless there are other matters, we will bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm wondering, Your Excellencies, would it be acceptable, given that this is the seventh witness that I'm examining this week and I cannot complete my cross-examination today, would it be acceptable that we hear the witness in examination-in-chief and that I start and finish my cross-examination on Monday next week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Ms. Edgerton? Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand the impact on the schedule would be minimal, given the time of the day and the length of the examination-in-chief. We don't have any adverse position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we'll accommodate your request, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's bring in -- so, Ms. Edgerton, please call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're bringing in the witness, I just wanted to let you know I won't be here on Monday, as I indicated to the Chamber, and my apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, I think I took this for granted, but I assume that the Defence would be prepared to still provide the documents they intend to use in cross-examination once the examination-in-chief is completed, pursuant to the Rule. I -- except -- maybe there's further preparation, there may be some additional documents but [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I see the nodding of Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good evening, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. Could you give us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ibro Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, you have no problem hearing me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then, Mr. Osmanovic, I'd like to ask you, do you remember meeting representatives from this Tribunal for the first time in 1994 and giving a statement to them about what happened in Vlasenica to you and your family during the war?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And since that time, you've testified here at the Tribunal about these things in five cases, and I'll list them: The Dragan Nikolic case in 1995; the Dusan Tadic case in 1996; the Slobodan Milosevic case in 2003; the Momcilo Krajisnik case in 2004; and the Stanisic and Zupljanin case in 2010. Do I have those right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in Bosnia in 2009, you also gave evidence to the state court there in the trial of Predrag Basta; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Predrag Bastah with an H at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then -- and recently, you've listened to audio recordings of those proceedings and re-read the transcript of your evidence in the Bastah trial; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then the day before yesterday, on 23rd of August, you listened to an interpreter read back to you another statement consolidating all this evidence you have given into one chronologically organised statement; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you did that, you made some clarifications, you corrected some things, and you gave some additional information which was then written down in this statement, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then after hearing that statement and taking into account the changes that you made, are you satisfied that it's an accurate record of what happened to you during the war as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if you were asked all those same questions that you were asked during the first interview in 1994 and all the earlier proceedings, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, given that the witness's amalgamated statement of 23 August is 65 ter number 90266, could that be the next Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P3212.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll go to the summary now of that written evidence. This witness was born and raised in Vlasenica, working as a factory worker and a volunteer firefighter. Around 22 April 1992, the town was taken over by the JNA Novi Sad Corps, assisted by local armed Serbs. Overnight the JNA moved in and by early morning these combined Serb forces had occupied municipality and other buildings, services, even factories. The JNA brought in armoured vehicles. The witness saw four tanks near the local stadium. Early that morning, a police vehicle announced via a loud-speaker that all weapons must be surrendered by 9.00 a.m. and the JNA would use force on those who failed to comply. Weapons were surrendered. A curfew was established. Non-Serbs were arrested by Serbian forces, and freedom of movement was restricted. People could not move about the town or leave the municipality without passes issued by the Serbian Crisis Staff. The witness's mother requested a pass to leave but was told it would only be issued if she signed a form voluntarily surrendering her rights to her home. She refused to sign the surrender form and never received a pass to leave Vlasenica. She remained in her apartment until she was taken to Susica camp. The JNA left Vlasenica around --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the Prosecutor please slow down a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, my apologies. The JNA left Vlasenica around 17 or 18 May of 1992, leaving their equipment behind for local Serb forces, who began attacks on Muslim villages. The witness learned from survivors that the villages of Pijuci, Dzamdzici and Bare were shelled and burned. Villagers were killed in the attacks. On 22 May 1992, the witness was arrested and detained with other Muslim men in the police station at Vlasenica. This began a period of detention that spanned 14 months and across four different facilities listed in Schedule C of the indictment in this case. From the police station, the witness went to the municipality prison in Vlasenica, Susica camp, and finally Batkovic, in Bijeljina, where he ultimately remained until he was exchanged in July 1993. In the Vlasenica police station, the witness learned from other detainees about the attack on the Muslim village of Zaklopaca by Serb forces. He speaks of the conditions in the jail, constant beatings of he and the other prisoners -- pardon me, of the conditions in the police station. Constant beatings of he and the other prisoners, torture, and killings perpetrated by members of the police forces, among others. At the municipality prison, the experience was much the same. In the prison, which would normally accommodate 50 people, there were about 150 detainees, all Muslims. Prisoners were taken out by Serb forces. A group of just over 30 men, 20 of whom were from the witness's own cell, were taken away on 2nd of June. The witness knows of only three survivors. While detained, the witness and other prisoners were taken under guard to the Muslim settlement of Drum where they buried the bodies of 22 civilian men. All but one had a single gun-shot wound between the eyes. The witness was moved to Susica, a facility commanded by Dragan Nikolic. He estimates there were more than 500 people detained there. Those he knew were Muslim. The witness recounts his experiences and those of the other detainees of the desperate conditions at Susica. There was no hygiene. Prisoners were constantly maltreated. He speaks -- the witness speaks of beatings, torture, and killings at the hands of Nikolic himself, guards, and members of the Serb police forces. He saw some of his fellow prisoners die after being beaten. He saw Nikolic beat a detainee so badly that person begged to be killed. He saw Nikolic put his bayonet in the mouth of one prisoner, and on another occasion saw Nikolic put his pistol in the mouth of another detainee; Nikolic then cocked the gun and pulled the trigger. The witness was moved to Batkovic at the end of June 1992. His younger brother, also detained at Susica, was kept behind, a camp official told him as a guarantee in case the witness ran away. He never saw his brother again. There were close to 3.000 prisoners from -- in Batkovic from locations all across Bosnia and Herzegovina, non-Serbs. There, again, the witness gives evidence of beatings, torture, and killings of the detainees by the Serb guards. A special group of prisoners was particularly singled out for beating and mistreatment. Under the eyes of Serb guards, three non-Serb detainees also took part in brutalities against the prisoners. Of the witness's immediate family, only two remain alive today. He's still searching for 33 members of his extended family from Vlasenica. And that's the summary of the written evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Osmanovic, I'd actually like to go to only one document, 65 ter number 11294, if we could call that up, please. You referred to that in your amalgamated statement at paragraph 157, which is your evidence about this document excerpted from your testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case. It's a photocopy of a list of persons detained at Batkovic, stamped and certified on 29 July 1999 by the Bijeljina lower court as being identical to the original. We could display the first page of this document in English, and after that, because this is a name list, I don't think we need to go to the translation. Mr. Witness, did you have a chance to have a detailed look at this document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go first over to e-court page 138 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you have a look, Mr. Osmanovic, at entry 21. Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to take you to a few pages in this document that you've looked at. If we could go back over to page 3, starting at the front of the document. And while we wait for that, Mr. Witness, do you remember at paragraphs 156, 164, 170, and 171 of your statement referring to someone by the name of Fadil Alihodzic as being one of the group of special prisoners singled out for constant beatings at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, that's Fadil Alihodzic, son of Ismet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you have a look at entry number 38, please, on this page and tell us then if you recognise the name there.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Number 38, Ismet Alihodzic -- Fadil Alihodzic, son of Ismet, brought from Vlasenica, and he was in this group intended for the beatings, as they used to refer to it as a special group.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your statement at paragraph 85, you referred to someone with the surname Boric, where you noted that only three men survived from that group of people that was taken out of the Vlasenica prison one night by Predrag Bastah and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, on what, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's being properly translated to me, I think that the Prosecutor said: You know that only a few survived. I'm afraid that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think she was referring to the para 89 and the witness noted only three men survived. Shall we take a look at para 85. "Out of this group of men, I found only three of them at Susica camp ..." Is this the passage you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes it is, indeed, and I thought I had got the paragraph numbering wrong, but I see I didn't. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he say that only these three survived?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The second-to-last sentence says -- the second-to-last sentence says: "I found only three of them at Susica camp."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I misspoke, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in paragraph 85, you said you found only three of those men at Susica camp. Now, I wonder if we could, please, go to page 13 of this document, 11294.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The previous list of Batkovic camp, 11294.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Page 13. Could we just keep with the original B/C/S version of that document, please. Is that e-court page 13? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to entry number 8, Mr. Witness. Do you recognise the name there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Nezir Boric, son of Ibro, used to live in Vlasenica. Upon my arrival at Susica, he was one of the persons that I have found there as one of the survivors.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you learn what happened to the men in that group that were taken out on the 2nd of June?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Of the three that I found at Susica camp, I heard that the bus with the rest of them proceeded towards Debelo Brdo. After the war, they were found and properly buried in the first burial that took place in Vlasenica and those were the people from that very same group.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we move on, please, to page 53, entries number 20 and 23. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There, Mr. Witness, we see the names Hajrudin and Hasim Ferhatovic. And I note in your statement you referred to Hajrudin and Hasim Ferhatovic as two brothers who were directed to bury bodies of two persons who died at Susica. Are these the same persons?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go over to page 94, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Entry number 11, we see the name of Medin Kolarevic, also from Vlasenica. Now, Mr. Witness, at paragraph 139 of your statement, you talk about the killing of Muharem Kolarevic at Susica camp and refer to his son named Medin, saying he was also at Susica and sent to Batkovic. Is this the same person?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Muharem Kolarevic was killed at Susica. His son, Medin, was with him there at Susica. And after that, the two of us went together to Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Based on the father's name and date of birth that you see on this document, do you find this to be the same Medin Kolarevic you refer to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, at paragraph 125, you refer to someone by the name of Reuf Rasidagic, who was beaten by Dragan Nikolic five times over five days. Now, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we then go over to page 151 of this document, please, entry number 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name you see there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Reuf Rasidagic, son of Rifet, is the person whom Dragan Nikolic beat as soon as he arrived at the Susica camp. And he asked me to tell you when was he last in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat. The interpreters didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, the interpreters were not able to hear you. Could you kindly repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Reuf Rasidagic, son of Rifet, is the person beat by Dragan Nikolic at Susica camp every day. He asked him to lie to him and tell him when was he last in China. Rasidagic asked him to kill him and the response Nikolic gave was: A bullet for you would be too costly because it costs us 3 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you also talked in your statement about a gypsy from Zenica by the name of Dzemal Zahirovic at paragraph 122, 170, and 171. Could we go in this list to page 189 and look at entry number 3. Do you recognise the name you see at entry number 3, Mr. Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what name is that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Dzemal Zahirovic of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it the same person you referred to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, also in your statement, you described Batkovic as holding groups of detainees from Kalesija, Vlasenica, Koraj, Zvornik, Brcko, Brezevo Polje, Trnovo, Divic, Bosanski Samac, Sanski Most, Rogatica, and Bijeljina, and we find all those names in paragraph 153. In reviewing this list, did you see groups of people from these locations that you had identified?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your statement you talked about a group of 512 prisoners coming from Batkovic from Manjaca after it was closed down sometime in December 1992 or January 1993, and that's at paragraph 154. Now, in that regard, I'd just like to go over to page 127 of this document. Now, do you see on this page a list of people who arrived at Batkovic from Kljuc, Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kotor Varos on -- all on the same day, on 13 December 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does that refresh your memory as to the date when prisoners from Manjaca might have arrived at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We returned from Lopare, from where they had taken us to work just before the new year, around the 19th of December. These people were already at Batkovic camp when I arrived. When they left -- when I left they weren't there. They were in a separate hangar. They slept in a separate hangar. Only the people who were giving out food had access to the other hangar, and from them I heard that 512 of them had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So now based on everything that we've talked about today and your review of this document, would you say that the list is an accurate one, Mr. Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we tender, then, 11294, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3213, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to ask you some things about your family. You've mentioned your younger brother, Hajrudin, in your statement at paragraphs 55, 100, 148, 150, and 193. And you spoke -- referred to some of your other family members. In paragraph 193, you spoke about your older brother, who you said was killed on 22 September 1992, who remains missing. Can you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Hakija was his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How do you know he -- how did you learn he was killed on 22 September 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: When the war ended, his wife, who is an ethnic Serb, came to visit my mother and she said that in September 1992, on the 22nd of September, 1992, he was killed. Unfortunately, we haven't found him yet. We don't know where he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraphs 100 and 193 of your written evidence, you spoke about what happened to your younger sister, who you said was 16 in 1992. Could you tell us her name?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Ferida.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you said her burnt remains were located at Pelemis, and I'd just like to know do you have any idea how far Pelemis is from Susica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: About 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what is Pelemis, do you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Pelemis is a Serb settlement where there was a four-year elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it still in Vlasenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, that belongs to the municipality of Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you learn how your younger sister, who you said had remained, in your written evidence, at Susica, did you learn how she came or how her remains came to be in the location of Pelemis?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived from Batkovic camp, I found Sabic Delva, a lady who was a neighbour of mine. She said that she was together with her and they were taken off the bus when they were being transported to Kladanj. Delva is an older woman who was released and my sister stayed there. When the mass grave at Pelemis was exhumed 7 and a half per cent of my sister's bones were found; the rest were burned, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did your neighbour tell you who took she and your sister off the bus?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you aware, apart from your neighbour, of any other survivors from Pelemis?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know of anyone else who had survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Finally, do you think, Mr. Osmanovic, you could put into words for the Judges how losing the family members you talk about in your statement and the members of your extended family and your experiences being detained have affected you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It cannot be described in words. It is very hard. You stay all alone. There is no one to open the door for you. You're picking through bones, hoping that you'd at least find that. I managed to find my brother's head 25 kilometres away from his body. His throat had been slit, and I found only 7 and a half per cent of my sister's bones, nothing more than that. It is very hard to describe this in words. However, I hope that there will be justice. I am not the one to mete out justice, but I hope that justice will catch up with those who did this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Osmanovic, I don't have any other questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd like now to tender the associated exhibits listed in our final notification of yesterday, 24 August. Some of those, Your Honour, were the subject of an order you issued in relation to KDZ-033 at the beginning of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Among the suggested associated exhibits, can I draw your attention to 65 ter 14240 and 00584 which were discussed in para 115. If you go to his -- para 115 in his amalgamated statement, he says: "Even though they are dated a few days before I arrived there, the number of detainees listed as in this document is consistent with what I remember seeing when I arrived at Susica." But if you look at those documents, those documents do not contain such information at all. I wonder, there is a mistake. Shall we upload 1584, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There may have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 of this document, Your Honours, refers to 640 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Also referring, Your Honour, to 620, which is crossed out, and 640, handwritten, prisoners. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- the witness's comments, Your Honour, of course confine to the number of prisoners being reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in relation to other associated exhibits, I noted that you added some new information recently in the final notification.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. They will all be admitted and given numbers in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, given the time, we are minded to rise for this week. And since we are not going to sit tomorrow, we'll resume on Monday next week, 29th, at 9.00, but probably you were explained by the Victims and Witnesses Section. Please do not discuss about your testimony with anybody else during those -- during that break. Do you understand, Mr. Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please have a nice weekend. 9.00 on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 29th day of August, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.43 p.m.,
